Аn important thing when approaching Blasphemous is managing your expectations.
At first glance it's easy to mislabel Blasphemous. It's a soulslike! It's a metroidvania! It's worse than Hollow Knight! It's not what made Souls good!

The description of the game paints it a "punishing action-platformer", and it's important to treat it as such. It falls short of a few important Metroidvania expectations, it (deliberately) doesn't have the very mobile combat of Hollow Knight, and it's definitely not the Dark Souls of anything, though it does borrow familiar elements.
If I absolutely had to come up with a genre description, I'd go with something silly like "atmospheric platformer". Do try Blasphemous if the thought of immersing yourself in a beautiful mysterious world appeals to you, a world that takes some mental effort to piece together. It is by no means style over substance, but it's not the amount of mechanical "substance" you expect coming from games like Dead Cells, or Hollow Knight, or maybe Valdis Story.

It's a fairly simple game in most terms, but with a slight tinge of 90s game design mixed in. Expect great music, an interesting setting and a strong presentation, and let the rest speak for itself without prejudice.

[i]Blasphemous[/i] is a metroidvania with more style than substance—but enough of the latter to be a great experience for lovers of the genre. It's also surprisingly easy to break into aspects, so here goes:

[b]Art:[/b] Stellar. It's not often that you get to immerse yourself in a pixel art world inspired by Goya and medieval religious art. Every second is a delight, and some visual imagery is mind-blowing (you don't want to know what happens to that bull).

[b]World/Narrative:[/b] Obscure and intriguing—more [i]Darkwood[/i] than [i]Dark Souls[/i], really, although all of these games feature people inexplicably turning into trees. I very much appreciate how heavy the Catholic inspiration is, going well beyond the common dark fantasy fare with the many-headed seraphs, flagellants, genuflection, torture devices... and lack of any actual crucifixes. It's dark, insane, pious, and filled with pain. I love it.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] Fine, but clunky. I died way too many times to the game not registering the jump command, and some puzzles/challenges become silly because of this. The game would have benefiited greatly if instant death was replaced with health loss, a la [i]Hollow Knight[/i], because it's infuriating when you die because your command didn't click with the geometry.

The level design is your standard metroidvania fare. It makes you lose yourself in the world successfully, and secrets are plentiful enough to warrant attentive exploration. The bosses are imaginative, different, and relatively easy. The music is great.

All in all, this game is simpler yet more beautiful and sadomasochistic than most fellow souls-like-ish metroidvanias ([i]Salt and Sanctuary, Death's Gambit[/i]). It will most certainly be a delight for those who love the genre. For those who don't... perhaps it might be better to start with [i]Hollow Knight[/i].

[h1]Sorrowful Be the Gamer[/h1]

If you're like me—impatient, easily bored, historically bad at video games, and somehow still convinced you could enjoy them—Blasphemous is here to torment and ultimately convert you.

This game slapped me so hard with its spiked censer that I came out the other side a changed person. I now have patience (??), better timing (??), and an emotional attachment to a man in a pointy hat who never speaks but suffers so beautifully.

I died. A lot. So often it could’ve been its [i]own[/i] achievement. I lost all my Tears of Atonement trying to retrieve my guilt, was impaled by every spike imaginable, and got relentlessly demolished by That Bull Thing™. I ragequit, came back, died again—and somehow loved every minute of it.

[hr]

[h2]Graphics[/h2]
Absolutely gorgeous. From bloodstained cathedrals to haunting pixel-lit skies, the art direction is visually divine. The Penitent One’s hat is a 10/10 fashion choice. There is drip in the penance.

[h2]Music[/h2]
Dear god. The soundtrack drenched me in misery. Atmospheric and hauntingly beautiful, it drags you into the depths of Cvstodia with no hope of return.
Special shoutout to Miriam’s Challenge music—it genuinely made me lose my mind. I might be humming it in my grave someday.

[h2]Lore[/h2]
Confusing at first, especially if you have memory issues or the attention span of a damp sponge (me). It’s all hidden in item descriptions, cryptic NPC dialogue, and the corpses of people who seem weirdly chill about being dead. But on my second run and NG+, it started to click—and I was hooked.
It’s twisted, tragic, and disturbingly beautiful.

[quote]“For twisted are, were, and will be, the paths of the Miracle.”[/quote]

Trauma. Suffering. I love it.

[h2]Highlights[/h2]

- Constant emotional damage  
- Miserable, beautiful women (Laudes, I love you)  
- The world [i]hurts[/i], but in a good way  
- Actually improved my patience, somehow  
- Killed by stairs. Repeatedly.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
[b]10/10 would get spiritually destroyed again. (Which I will, time for my 3rd run.)[/b]
[i]Sorrowful be the heart, penitent ones.[/i]

[hr]
In the brotherhood of penitents. Straight up "blaspheming it". and by "it", haha, well, let's just say... Mea Culpa.

I'm going to be completely transparent with this review. I believe I enjoyed to game overall, but my feelings are carried mostly by the game's atmosphere, characters, story, and art style. The core game play constantly annoyed and bored me. I enjoyed the game the most when exploring new areas. The areas and scenery are amazing. The story is interesting to follow, although I found myself getting bored near the end with constant backtracking. Metroidvania's are supposed to excel with backtracking, but this game makes it feel like a chore. You will run all the way to the beginning of the game, just to open a door and have a single platform section while your expectations were much higher. The enemies are very well designed, but some become annoying walls that force you to stop and fight each time you want to pass. However my biggest gripe is with the bosses. I have played my share of souls-like games and I understand the importance of the bosses.  The bosses in this game are amazing visually, but the fight itself is very unsatisfying. You are basically fighting meat bags that  take hit after hit while you only have a few choices of attacks. Most of the late game bosses turn into hit-and-run strategies. You get very small opening of attacks and they punish you for going for a full combo. When it comes to the final hit that kills the boss, I felt more satisfied that it was over rather than satisfied that I killed a "hard boss." The worst thing about this was how contrast the final boss was to the rest. It was a literal pushover. After I fought it, I was staring at the screen saying "that's it?" The true ending at least adds on to the fight, but it only helps so much. 

-----------------------------------TLDR-----------------------------------

PROS: Amazing scenery, atmosphere, art style, character/enemy design

CONS: Boring repetitive combat, lack of mobility, unsatisfying bosses extremely underwhelming final boss fight.

Basically get the game if you don't need to have an engaging combat system. The story and world that you explore makes this game good enough for purchasing and trying out.

[h1]“For twisted are, were, and will be, the paths of the miracle.”[/h1]

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
[b]This review is based on playing on the Steam deck.[/b]
[b]Blasphemous[/b] is a brutal 2D metroidvania/souls-like amalgamation about the burdens of devotion and honour and what it takes to achieve your goals despite a world cast against you. With a heavy focus on cerebral combat, precision timing and understanding your skills [b]Blasphemous[/b] attempts to take the mantle of genre classic, but does it have what it takes? So take up your blade, steel yourself with your faith and discover a land that seeks penance or be the one to make it fall to the hungering darkness that awaits the hopeless.

[table]
[tr]
	[th][b]🟩 Positives[/b][/th]
	[th][b]🟥 Negatives[/b][/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
	[td]🟩 There are few means of fighting the vast army of foes that stand in your way. You must become familiar with your limited arsenal and how to best utilise it to succeed.

🟩 The map is large but not overly. There are several biomes to explore, plenty of secrets to uncover and items in abundance to collect.

🟩 Bosses are not only significantly powerful beings. They are also unique experiences to discover, with each being vastly different from the last.

🟩 A wonderfully unique art style that depicts sadness through pixelated forefront and painted background scenery to create an immersive environment.

🟩 And lastly: an immaculate audio selection that accompanies the journey, with excellent sound effects and a song for every situation that captures the moment astoundingly well.
[/td]
	[td]🟥 Despite how fun the boss fights are, they peak in challenge very early into the game, and the title becomes substantially easier until the end.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

[h1]Story[/h1]
The once prosperous lands of Cvstodia have fallen from on high at the hands of a foul curse that has come to be known as The Miracle.

You take control of the Penitent One as he awakens from the dead to bear witness to the massacre of his brothers and sisters for opposing the church he once served. With the sacred blade Mea Culpa, he must travel across this tainted world, purging it of its corruption and bringing penance to now-dying lands that embody it.

I genuinely adored the story written here. A tragic tale that cradles you from the moment you start the journey to the moment it ends, delivering you an account of betrayal and vengeance, and as the screen goes dark for the last time, you are left to contemplate if the fight was worth the victory.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
[h3]Requiem Aeternam[/h3]
You will spend most of your time in Blasphemous fighting against the people and creatures that call Cvstodia home, so it is best to become acquainted with the mechanics of how to do so effectively as quickly as possible.

🟩 You have very few means of self-defence early into the game, so you will become familiar with dodging, parrying and counter striking at opportune moments. Firstly, evading is the most straightforward and useful tool because completely removing yourself from the path of danger is the safest method to keep living. The alternate approach that is far more critically timed is the parry mechanic, where you remain at risk to perfectly time a block, stun the enemy and allow a window for you to counterstrike.

🟩 You will slowly build an array of magical abilities as you discover them in hidden and secret places that can be useful in giving you an edge in combat. They vary from buffs to more versatile damage spells.

🟩 Lastly, and probably the most important tool on your belt, is the sword you have in your hand. The Mea Culpa is a sacred blade that starts pretty weak despite how it looks but will gradually get stronger until it becomes as feared as it should be. You upgrade its versatility at shrines located across Cvstodia and by spending Tears of Atonement, which serves as the currency in Blasphemous.

🟥 Boss encounters will be your greatest challenge in testing your growing abilities, as they vary from relatively simple in both method and style to far more complex and challenging. My one major bugbear lies here as there is a rather steep difficulty curve early on, but once past that, the rest of the game becomes spectacularly easy.

[h3]Detestatio Sacrorum[/h3]
🟩 The remainder of the experience will entail you exploring the world, and there is a literal plethora of secrets across the game to locate, varying from collectibles to story-related key items and lore-related entries, to name a few.

🟩 These items can help you unlock some seriously invaluable powers which will greatly assist you on your travels, and for the truly vigilant, it can deliver you a new ending.

🟩 Thankfully throughout your journey you will have access to an ever updating map that provides a lot of helpful information you can utilise to traverse the world and locate those pesky hidden items you may have missed. The map also marks specific places of interest and allows you to add your own custom markers as points of reference.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3014194923

[h1]Audio and Visual[/h1]
[b]Blasphemous[/b] is probably one of the more eye-catching Metroidvania games I have ever had the chance to experience as it has a firm grasp on a very classic retro style in both how it looks and plays, but at the same breath, the beautifully drawn backgrounds are astounding to take in. 

It is also extremely graphic despite its style, and I would not recommend anyone drastically underage to play this title as many of the themes are extremely adult in nature.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3014195305

The audio is much the same, and it wasn't till about 5 or 6 hours into the game that I realised how amazingly the sound effects coupled with the sad, down-trodden music that echoes through your ears in each new biome.

[h1]Deck Performance and Specifications[/h1]
The deck delivered the seamless experience I've come to expect of the device whilst playing [b]Blasphemous[/b]. The game had no graphical or technical issues to report whatsoever.

With the game set to default for the deck, the battery consumption was fair, giving about five hours of life from a full charge.

[h1]Final Thoughts - Excellent[/h1]
[url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2529084785]Review chart here.[/url]
To say that I have played a lot of Metroidvania games in my life would be a severe understatement, and I am an avid and appreciative fan of the souls and souls-like genre, I wanted this to be clearly known, so when I say that [b]Blasphemous[/b] for me was amongst the best experiences, I've had within either of these genres in the past. The whole formula just worked really well for me, and despite some rather small difficulty issues, this was an exceptionally compelling journey that I hope to re-experience numerous times over the years. A worthwhile purchase at any price.

[quote] Climbing to the peak of Cvstodia isn’t as easy as going to [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/41449676/] Summit Reviews[/url], where the reviews are of the highest quality.[/quote]

[quote]If your heart still be filled with sorrow, Penitent One, and your faith be stripped to naught, don't fear for your soul, for [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/43064204/] Hell, Purgatory and Paradise[/url] will deliver you to salvation.[/quote]

That totally [i]metal[/i] aesthetic you see in the trailer doesn't quit for the entire thing.  It's just short of unbelievable that there could be so much exquisitely gothic and hypnotically gory pixel art in a [i]single[/i] indie game, but devotion can accomplish great things indeed -- case in point, the hero of this fine production, who routinely takes down baddies several times his size in pursuit of his religious (and totally [b]metal![/b]) pilgrimage.  The gameplay is as good as the graphics, if you can believe that; it's not slow, not fast, too dynamic to be "deliberate," highly responsive on the dodge/parry front, and has a fair amount of wiggle room for failure.  [i]Blasphemous[/i] is a more than serviceable metroidvania that won't stress you out [i]too[/i] much with its platforming, exploration, or boss fights -- but it's not exactly a cakewalk, either, and of course you can replay the thing in "torment" mode if you feel like it.  The game is fairly short -- just take a look at my playtime, and shave off an hour or so for when I had to ALT-TAB for other things -- but with something interesting and fun every few seconds, it's an experience well worth paying for. 

"Ye olde mysterious Soulsborne breadcrumb lore" is there in plenty, but I couldn't really connect with it; it's a device I've grown quite weary of, and I think it might even be a little more incoherent in [i]Blasphemous[/i] than in other games.  Suffice to say that the Grievous Miracle raped the land of Cvstodia and its people one eventful day, transforming many of them into self-mortifying mutants with a quasi-Catholic theme.  Got it?  That's really all you need to know, as far as I'm concerned.  But though the story is sadly non-existent for me, the excellent gameplay and strong visual themes more than serve their purpose.

[h1]A Punishing Metroidvania with a Fantastic, Grotesque Setting[/h1]

It took me a while to really *get* this game but in the end I loved it! Let's break down some pros and cons.

[b]Pros[/b]

1. Incredible setting and art direction. Cvstodia is 15th century Catholic Spain on steroids. The sense of dread is palpable, the fervor of the characters is overwhelming and the brutality on display is gruesome. The pixel art is on point and the monster design is almost aggressively original and intensely horrifying.
2. Intriguing story. From my experience, most Metriodvanias don't really have an expansive plot, preferring instead to let the gameplay take the spotlight, but Blasphemous has a very engaging, and very mysterious, premise. Piecing together the lore is a game unto itself.
3. Tight combat. It can take a while to get used to as the player character moves like a truck but if you take the time to really learn it, you'll find there's a very deliberate and rewarding combat system in Blasphemous.
4. The music. Dark and somber, the music is a great accompaniment to the levels.
5. Fantastic dev team and DLCs. These guys are amazing. Not only did they work their asses off to patch this game but they also added three free DLCs.

[b]Cons[/b]

1. Frustrating platforming. Honestly, platforming isn't Blasphemous' strong suit. The player character is slow and clumsy and the amount of insta-kill spikes and sudden pitfalls, and the subsequent slog back to that location from the nearest save point when you inevitably die, can be extremely tiring. This wouldn't have been so egregious if the game wasn't so fond of putting these traps everywhere.
2. Bugs. Even with all the patching, there are still bugs present. Imprecise movement, animation glitches and screen gray-outs are just some of the frustrations I've experienced. Thankfully, there wasn't any game breaking bug.
3. Annoying enemies. Funnily enough, I found the bosses in this game to be on the easier side with a few exceptions that can stun lock you. What was really grating was the amount of enemies with cheap attacks like those dudes throwing crosses.

[b]Conclusion[/b]

All in all, while Blasphemous isn't perfect, it's a must play for anyone who enjoys Metroidvanias or finds the setting/plot interesting. Hopefully, we'll get more amazing games from the devs in the future.

PS: Do yourself a favor and play with Spanish audio. It's SOOOOO much more atmospheric that way,

Buy this game if you:
-Want a gratifying combat experience
-Don't mind back-tracking
-Get high levels of satisfaction from exploration
-Aren't too faint of heart
-Have an appreciation for atmosphere-complimenting music
-Can get past a few minor bugs
-Like to feel rewarded for your efforts
-Have a good memory
-Enjoy the overall aesthetic

I've played this since release week, and I can confidently say the gameplay has been polished and the bugs ironed out over its updates. Anything you might've heard about the game being a buggy mess or having janky gameplay is mostly untrue by now (bugs still remain here and there but they aren't too frequent anymore, and certainly not game-breaking like before).

Gameplay: Tight and responsive, can quickly cancel almost any animations to slide away or block an attack. Polished over the updates it's received. Difficulty is just right for those familiar with videogames and platformers. New NG+ and challenge modes have easily doubled or tripled the replayability of the game. Allows some diversity in playstyle by equipping different items and NG+ challenge modes. A fair number of quests of varying difficulty.

Plot/lore: Plentiful item descriptions to read, filled with lore. Very mature plot. Different from your repetitive old dark fantasy tales, this takes inspiration from religious and Spanish themes.

Art: Absolutely phenomenal and detailed pixel art. Smooth animations. Cutscenes could do with a little better frame rate but there aren't many anyway.

Voice acting: You [b]HAVE[/b] to play it dubbed in [b]SPANISH[/b] (just turn on English subs to understand), because the cast this game's got is AAA quality, despite being an indie game. I'm impressed with how they managed to gather all that talent and money. English dub was recently improved, but you'd be a heretic to play it that way.

Bosses: They're pretty challenging and generally feel good to fight, with only a few exceptions.

Soundtrack: It's both amazing while you're playing, and outside of the game. You won't hear such fantastic Spanish tunes in any other game. Loved it.

Map: A pretty well thought-out map, allows you to take it on from different sides, true to the Metroidvania genre. However, you don't need to find new abilities to gain access to following levels, but instead they allow you acquire more loot, upgrades and find new shortcuts. NG+ especially lets you keep your abilities so you can take on even more radical routes around the place.

This was my first platformer and tbh i was never too interested in the genre, but the visuals alone in this made me wanna give it a try. And let me just say, the art is absolutely stunning, this is probably one of the most gorgeous and stylistic games i've ever seen, i have a love for pixel art, so this game just had me in awe. The animations, enemy designs, map designs, boss aesthetics. its such a visually striking game and i honestly cant praise the artists enough.

As for gameplay i enjoyed it for the most part. Some bosses were ridiculously difficult though, might be partly my fault for being kinda ass, but i felt the mechanics for some to be slightly unfair n cheap tbh. i.e the massive uncontrollable knock backs, enemy attacks mixed w unblockable projectiles, stunlocks, enemies attacking while flying off the screen etc. Overall this game is FRUSTRATING, like hair pulling levels of frustration sometimes, almost as if the devs purposefully made it to be as annoying and non forgiving as possible, whoever decided to add insta-killing spikes, i literally dispise u with all my heart lol. 

Another downside was how much I had to look up stuff. Figuring out certain quests was a borderline chore at times because of how cryptic n vague some of them were, plus the many obscure secrets and hidden areas that felt impossible to find on your own unless you got super lucky, like hitting a random blank wall to unlock a hidden room. It just isnt realistic and so many will miss out on cool items.

I also found it quite strange how dummy linear the game wants you to go in order for you to achieve a "good" ending, it feels nearly impossible to get this ending w/o looking it up. On top of that, the "bad" ending was pretty disappointing imo. Checked out the good ending on yt and it looks 1000x better, which sucks even more knowing that like 90% of the players will probably only ever see the bad one in their first run. It just don't make sense to me at all.

I still had a fun time overall tho. Despite the frustrating parts, many of the boss fights were still enjoyable, navigating around the map while finding new items n areas was a bit annoying in certain areas but still very fun, story was a bit confusing at times but still super cool, music was also surprisingly good aswell, and I’ll honestly never forget how stunning the art is. This game definitely has its issues tho, and i honestly just wish they didn't make this game so purposefully frustrating and punishing for the average player, but ig that's just the way it is 7.5/10

Story: It's easy to create a story based on religion. It takes great creativity and skill to make it feel like a homage, like a confession and like a collective memory. The language may be a bit difficult to understand sometimes, but granted, if you listen carefully, all your questions will be answered and you will be satisfied with the amount of lore behind every sentence. 

Sound: Music is absolutely breathtaking, it quickly became one of my favourite OSTs of all time. Hits very deep. Sounds are satisfying and immersive.

Gameplay: Spikes are the biggest boss of this game. Every other obstacle in the game can be deafeated or at least you can find a good way to avoid it, but insta death spikes will follow you until the end game and I HATE THEM. I love the combat, though not very complicated, it's solid and simply fun. Game is pretty ruthless and after dying a couple of times forces you to think about your build so you can explore other items and tactics. I did get sad after beating the bosses in 3 attempts max, but when I found out about the no heal challenge achievement, I spent much more time with them and it was more fun!

Overall feelings: I was born into a catholic family and many cutscenes and dialogues reminded me of how confused I was as a child when they made me repeat "my fault, my fault, my greatest fault" in the church. I'm not religious anymore, but the confusion came back when I played the game - what is even that fault? What are we repenting? Why being a martyr is the greatest thing that can happen to you in the eyes of God? I am completely fascinated when it comes to religion and thanatology, and Blasphemous checks out all the boxes for me. I can't wait to 100% this one and then go straight into Blasphemous 2.

[h2]A Solid Metroidvania With Souslike Elements[/h2]
[u]This review is from the perspective of someone who 100%s games on Steam[/u]

Blasphemous is by all means a good game. It has a great interconnected world that opens up as you upgrade, a solid combat system, a decent story, and some of the most metal enemy designs I have ever seen in a video game. Simply put… there is no one area of Blasphemous I would say is bad or falling behind. Unfortunately though, this game also has a lot of areas that I feel are so close to greatness, but find themselves falling a little bit short. As a certified yapper I will be breaking down all of it. The good and the bad. 

Again, I would like to highlight that I think this game is good and worth your time. While my review will be fairly balanced between good parts and bad parts, I would give this game overall an 8.5 / 10. Anyways… I will now go in-depth on several different aspects of the game including Story, Gameplay, MISC, and the Completion Experience. There will be minor spoilers for what the game contains, but I will not go into any specifics that would ruin your experience. 

[h2]Story[/h2]
I think the story and lore of Blasphemous is something that could be quite polarizing. There is a lot of lore to the world of Custoida, but unfortunately so much of it is hidden behind cryptic dialogue and item descriptions. I don’t like to make comparisons, but I think saying it is similar to Dark Souls 1 is probably the best way to help you understand what you are getting into. At the same time though, I honestly felt Dark Souls 1 had an easier plot to follow, at least on the surface level. 

So yeah, the story is a bit of a mixed bag for me. After beating the game I felt like I knew little of the overall lore and I personally did not enjoy that. After watching some lore videos though I can confidently say there is a rich world here, it just requires a bit more brain power then most games. Thankfully, this is probably something you already know if you personally find it to be a dealbreaker or not. My last point is that this game can easily be enjoyed without knowing the lore. 

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
There are two elements of gameplay I want to touch upon in this review; those being combat and world design. Let's start with combat.

Combat in Blasphemous is a good time. You only have one weapon throughout the game, but you do slowly unlock new skills and “prayers”, which allow you to customize a couple of your moves. For the most part I think this system works. The one weapon is well designed and feels good to use, and the couple of things you can unlock / customize allow for some slight build variety.  I do think there could have been more here though. Maybe having different weapons you could choose from or a more fleshed out skill tree is the solution, but as of right now, I just feel that your combat options don’t grow as much as they could. 

The other part of combat though is what you are fighting. Enemy variety is strong, with each enemy feeling unique and well-designed. The boss roster is solid, but I also think the game doesn’t have anything that really blew my socks off. The final boss is also, in my opinion, the worst boss in the game. There is one thing going for all the enemies / bosses in the game though, and that is their art design. Like damn did this team cook. I won’t go into too much detail so as to not spoil, but if you are into some messed up designs then this is the game for you. 

Moving onto world design.. It's great and I think I would deem this Blasphemous’ strongest trait. The world is fun to explore and it is interconnected in ways that you don’t seem often in video games. Smashing through a wall or dropping down a ladder to reach somewhere you’ve already been is a special feeling, and this game is full of moments like those. You can also access most of the map right away if you know where to go. This makes repeat playthrus a joy as you mess around with ways to sequence break. I do have one complaint though and that is with the relic system. Relics are what allow you to reach areas you couldn’t previously reach. Since this game doesn’t have anything that changes your movement mechanics, the game instead had you equip these relics to shift the world around you and open up new paths. It's a cool system, but unfortunately it has one issue, which is that you can only equip 3 of these relics at a time. I understand what they were going for, but all this results in is having you have to go into the menu to shift around which relics you have equipped whenever you reach a certain puzzle or area. It just is not engaging. For the most part though, the world design slaps. 

[h2]MISC[/h2]
I can not emphasis how much the art direction here slaps. Yes, I used slaps two sentences in a row, but simply put… some parts of this game do slap. The soundtrack is also worth mentioning. Its good!

[h2]Completion Perspective[/h2]
It took me around 25 hours to get 100% achievements. This game does require a fair amount to earn that blue badge including: at least 2 playthrus, collecting 100% of various different collectible items, exploring the entire map, completing some pretty complex npc questlines which can be failed, and 2 “challenge run” type achievements. 

Most of these are pretty doable, though I would recommend looking up a guide on your second playthru to ensure you progress the npc quests right. The two challenge runs require you to beat the first half of the game in less than 3 hours and beat all the original (no dlc) bosses without healing. I would recommend going for the no healing one first, as it is good prep for the speedrun one when you pursue that. I will say that the speedrun time is fairly forgiving. 

Overall, not a bad completion unless you refuse to use a guide. 

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
Blasphemous is a solid metroidvania. It gets so much right for a first game and if the sequel can just improve a little bit on this solid foundation, I might view it as one of the all-time greats. Anyways, I hope you enjoy your journey with Blasphemous!

P.S Feel free to friend request me on Steam if you want to keep up on my completionist journey!

The first time you see Blasphemous it makes a big impression; it’s violent, dark, gothic, and filled with twisted religious imagery. Its main character is certainly unique looking – clad in armor with a fierce looking cone helmet and wielding a jagged iron sword. Enemies are grotesque and the world is haunted. It’s 1997, and while the video game industry seems drunk on the notion that 3D technology will make 2D titles obsolete, we defiantly go out in evenings for pleasure as nights are still young. Twentytwo years it will take for the formula of [i]Castlevania: Symphony of the Night[/i] to find its way into another worthy, now pixel-perfect incarnation by a dream team out of Spain. [i]Blasphemous[/i] is a courageous scion: deep lore, engaging quests and puzzles, challenging but fair difficulty. Refreshingly, there isn’t an insult like the hand-holding so common these days, and never a tired trope.

The game is wildly imaginative in its narrative, environments and enemy pool. It’s all a twisted fever dream of Spanish religious and folklore history: that concept of taking something familiar and accentuating certain elements; here, it is the macabre inherent in these themes. At times, this feels like stepping into a Hieronymus Bosch painting come alive. Then, an excellent soundtrack ranging from melancholy Spanish melodies to foreboding mood pieces expertly complements a gorgeous hand-drawn presentation, that together with the often literature-level writing create an atmosphere that is a delight to get lost in.

Players will find a lot to do: for one, the large open-world map sports varied areas that are a joy to explore and come back to. So far, two DLCs that mostly feature Kickstarter stretch goals are included, and these add more quality content to the already complete base experience. There is, however, the awkwardly tone-deaf cross-promotion with [i]Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night[/i], that has Miriam of said title appear for a tepid minute.

The Game Kitchen – still actively supporting [i]Blasphemous[/i] – deserves respect for emptying heart and soul into their work. [i]Blasphemous[/i] is one of the few games at the very top of the 2D Slash ‘n’ Jump genre renaissance, the pedestrian rest trudging in ever-repeating circles in the mediocre far below. For those who can appreciate such a gem, rejoice. Nights are young once more, you know. Don’t miss out on this title.

Hoo boy... I just finished my first playthrough of this game and I wanted to immediately give my review.

First off, let's get the obvious out the way: this game is harder than eskimo nipples. Despite its difficulty, one very important aspect of the game that sets it apart from other metroidvania games is that when you die (and you will), it's not game over and losing all of your progress since your last save. Instead, you are brought back to your last save point with a minor debuff to your mana until you recover the spirit(?) of you dead body at the location of your death. There are a good amount of save points throughout the game so the trek back to your last death point should never be too far.

Speaking of traversing the map, this is one of the more tedious gameplay moments. Warp rooms are in very short supply, and since this is a metroidvania style game, you will be backtracking a lot. This can lead to some rather lengthy progression, especially if you aren't exactly sure where to go next. There is a method of unlocking the ability to fast travel between save points later on in the game but this upgrade is not made known to the player (it's unlocked via a very obscure method).

My absolute favorite thing about this game is the visuals. The pixel art cutscenes are brilliant and the grotesque religious imagery used throughout the entire game was so good that it actually gave me unsettling chills at some points (most notably some of the bosses). The music also perfectly compliments the theme of the game.

The boss fights are very well done with a solid variate of styles among them. They're all very challenging [spoiler]with the exception of the final boss, who was a pushover[/spoiler]. 

The story? Yeah, I have no idea. Good luck trying to follow this one. I was lost from the start.

Overall, it's 9/10 for me. The only thing stopping it from being 10/10 is how much of a nightmare this game is for a completionist like myself. Don't wait until it's on sale. This game is worth every penny of $24.99.

A beautiful and ruthless adventure in a world dominated by a distorted religion.

Blasphemous's most vital characteristic is its pixel art, blending gothic aesthetics with the game's brutal style. The scenes are captivating yet often frightening, featuring macabre entities and mysterious creatures. Spanish culture inspires blasphemous settings, the Middle Ages and Catholicism, represented by locations, enemies, symbols and more. These elements create a disconcerting but exciting universe.

"For twisted are, were, and will be, the paths of the miracle." 

Exploring this world is fascinating, with stone cathedrals, a leprosy-stricken village, and a mountaintop convent. The artist's gory and morbid imagery is inspired by violent Catholic iconography and Dolorism - a doctrine that exhorts to "suffer to atone for one's sins."
Some moments are so striking they motivate you to continue, eager to see what crazy visions lie ahead.

"Make my chest hurt with regret. Forge your punishment and nail it deep." 

The level design is well-developed, featuring shortcuts and secret passages. However, the platforming sections can become tedious due to instant-death thorns or bottomless abysses, forcing you back to the last save point and requiring repetitive travel. Despite this, exploration is generally a well-balanced challenge. The distance between save points forces careful progression, concentrating on each confrontation to avoid fatal errors. From these moments comes a sense of achievement commensurate with the effort made and great satisfaction at opening shortcuts, which are plentiful throughout the levels; these mark coherent design thought as whole and intelligently connected parts. The game alternates between vertical combat-focused rooms and horizontal platforming areas, making exploration an absolute pleasure.

"Go fearlessly, Penitent One." 

Combat is functional, with a simple action palette available from the start, except for a few unlockable special moves. You can perform a basic sword strike, parry, dodge, and jump over attacks. Giving three responses to opposing attacks - each enemy has an ideal response, learned through experience. Boss battles, however, require mastering their attack patterns. 

The game's combat and exploration mechanics are simple in their execution. It is complex regarding its inventory system - with several options that affect gameplay. An excellent example is the passive skill items that can be gained, called Rosary Beads. Some objects protect against poisoning and things that allow them to deal more damage or gain energy by breaking items in the scenario. There are also Relics, which grant the ability to see hidden platforms and hear voices from specific statues; Prayers are spells within this game; Hearts of Mea culpa add buffs to the sword through items found during our journey; Quest Items are abundant because of the several side quests available throughout the game; finally, there are Key Items which serve specific purposes like opening doors or unlocking treasure chests.

 "Sorrowful be the heart, Penitent One, full of clemency."

Death is inevitable but forgiving. Your Fervour bar, utilized for specialized techniques, will become capped more with each death. You will also receive a penalty to gain Tears (In-game currency). These penalties can be undone by returning to the place of death or visiting a specific location.

[b] Blasphemous [/b] is an awe-inspiring Metroidvania that captivates with its relentless challenge and hauntingly intricate world. As the Penitent One, you delve into the macabre, gothic landscapes of Cvstodia, teeming with grotesque monstrosities and meticulously designed platforming trials. The combat is visceral and unforgiving, demanding impeccable precision and skill, while the breathtaking pixel art and evocative soundtrack envelop you in a chilling tapestry of religious fervor and despair. The rich, enigmatic lore is seamlessly interwoven into the environment, rewarding meticulous exploration and curiosity. Despite its punishing difficulty, Blasphemous delivers a profoundly satisfying and unforgettable journey, making it an essential experience for aficionados of dark fantasy and rigorous action-platformers. Highly recommended!

When I first started Blasphemous, I honestly didn't like it.

My first thought was that it was just a "worse Hollow Knight" or Nine Sols. The game felt strange, the world was confusing, and I wasn't really sure what to think of it.

But I decided to push through and give it a chance.

And I'm really glad I did.

The further I got, the more this strange and fascinating world started pulling me in. The music and atmosphere were probably the biggest things that changed my opinion. After making my way toward the first real boss and getting my first major upgrade, I started realizing that Blasphemous was much bigger than I initially thought.

I wanted to explore more.

More importantly, I wanted to understand the world I was exploring.

The world of Blasphemous is cruel. Almost everyone seems to be suffering in some way, and it constantly made me question what exactly I was doing there. Was I actually the good guy? Was I just another part of this twisted world? Or was there something more behind the Penitent One's journey?

That mystery kept me playing.

The enemies and bosses generally don't feel completely overwhelming or "unkillable" in the way some Dark Souls bosses can feel. Most fights are challenging without feeling unfair, although there are definitely a few bosses that can take some time to overcome.

And I actually enjoyed that.

The NG+ DLC adds even more to this experience. Not only does it give you more challenges, but it also adds more story and helps paint a larger picture of the world when you play through the game again. For someone like me, who enjoys doing almost everything a game has to offer, it made going back for 100% feel worthwhile rather than simply being cleanup.

There is one part of the game that I really didn't enjoy, though: the platforming.

I'm not talking about the normal movement and jumping around the world. That part is fine. I'm talking about the specific platforming trials that force you into more awkward parkour sections.

There are five of these, and thankfully, you don't need to complete them.

But if you're like me and want to do almost everything in a game, even the small stuff, they can become pretty frustrating.

Despite that, I ended up really enjoying my time with Blasphemous.

It's not an easy game, but I wouldn't call it an extremely difficult one either. The biggest challenge, at least for me, was getting into the game in the first place.

I think Blasphemous becomes much more enjoyable once you stop comparing it to other Metroidvanias.

At first, I saw it as a worse Hollow Knight.

By the end, I was looking at it as Blasphemous.

And after completing the game, the NG+ DLC, getting Ending C, and finally reaching 100%, I feel pretty satisfied leaving this first journey behind.

Now it's time to see what Blasphemous 2 has waiting for me.

This game is not a quick hack and as it first appears; each encounter is about timing and knowing when to strike, block, or dodge. It’s a slower paced game when it comes to combat. Once I realized how I should play it and approach encounters, the game started to open up. As you explore, you’ll find items that increase your stats and make things a bit easier (relatively speaking). And then there’s the bosses… after a couple tries of getting stomped for each boss, you’ll learn their attack patterns and eventually beat them if you keep at it. The difficulty of this game would be very much at home in the early 90s. But the more you play, the better you get, the more rewarding it is.

The Level Design - feels quit simple and uninspired early on, but as you progress through the game and open up more areas, the level design does get much better with layout and complexity. As well as a few jumping puzzles thrown in for good measure.
The Art Style - is gorgeous, even for a retro style. The color palette for the variety of locations is well chosen. Every area had a unique visual theme.
The Sprite Animation - is well done and fluid overall. The animations for the executions you can perform on the enemies are… detailed.
The Music - is excellent and evokes the mood of each area well. It’s not a throwback to the midi sounds of the 90s, but rather has a more orchestral sound for the most part.
The Quests – the quest system I had some issues with. When you encounter characters or find items, you are sometimes given a vague hints or directions on where you should go - whether through dialogue or the item description. Most of the time you are given no hints as to the task. I had no idea what a quest item was for and would accidently stumbled upon completing a quest. Some areas you can only get to by getting special items as rewards for completing quests.
The Story – it seemed like a twisted take on Catholicism from the time of the Spanish Inquisition. The lore I found quite compelling and wanted to know more of what happened to this world. I found little snippets along the way from the lore on items or through character dialogue. The journey of the Penitent One to rid the world of the Grievous Miracle and take on the guilt of that world is interesting as it is twisted.
The Voice Acting – Overall it’s really well done. There's a character or two that just wasn't on par with the quality of the rest of the voice cast.

I’m not usually a completionist or one to write reviews, but this game really resonated with me and it was quite a fulfilling experience. After 27 hours of play and 99% completion (where’s that last 1%??), I finally beat the game and I’m glad I pressed through the initial difficulty curve. Can’t wait for the DLC!

There is perhaps no Spanish painter more influential than Francisco Goya. Although he was immortalized as one of the post-renaissance masters, the Primer Pintor de Camara’s life was anything but happy. It’s almost certain that the tragic death of his children and the turmoil of his country inspired the nightmarish works of his late career. Combine this with his relationship with Catholicism and you have the principal inspiration for Blasphemous.

Blasphemous is not a classical Metroidvania a la Symphony of the Night, and it’s not quite a Souls-like. To define it: it is a hack’n slash platformer with strong presentation. While the combat is rather simple, the visual design is anything but. The world of Cvstodia features some of the finest pixel art in the industry, ranging from grand cathedrals to grotesque abominations. Enemy variety is great and boss designs are reminiscent of the finest from series like Dark Souls. Complimenting this is strong world building and a macabre story dripping with religious symbolism. For el amor de Dios, please play in Spanish with subtitles on.

Not all works are blemish-free. Blasphemous' difficulty curve is bumpy, loot is unexciting, and magic is overtuned. There are also a few bugs, including Guilt Fragments in unreachable areas and the player getting stuck but they are rare. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2934161524 

Like Goya’s works, Blasphemous is uniquely beautiful and disturbing, and while it does not reach the lofty heights of the painter’s career, it is certainly worthwhile.

As a side-scrolling Soulsborne platformer, Blasphemous definitely has some competition in his genre, but it stands its own ground with its unique setting and aesthetics. While i consider its gameplay to be worse than Hollow Knight, it is by no means bad, and i happily admit that every hour i've spent on this game was one hour that has been well spent.

[b]Graphics[/b]

The setting's primarily inspired by catholic asceticism. Self-Mortification features heavily both graphically as well as narratively.  The visuals that are depicted are often grotesque and repugnant, yet the art and conveyance of said imagery has an uncanny beauty, resulting in a terrifyingly appropriate aesthetic to compliment the setting.

[b]Story[/b]

Storywise the game does a decent job of explaining itself, which is unusual for many Soulsborne games. Characters tend to speak plainly, defining their purpose and propositioning the aid of the main character in a relatively straightforward fashion. In turn, the story makes sense, and it is nothing if not unique. 

[b]Gameplay[/b]

Blasphemous has high quality in terms of gameplay. While it may be quite a bit slower than others of its ilk, the game still feels smooth and responsive. Some very useful mechanics are hidden behind hard-to-reach collectibles, which may be enjoyable for some people, but missing out on them severely handicaps the martial capacities of your character. As a primary feature in Soulsborne games, a mention goes out to the boss-fights: they are generally very enjoyable, providing good challenge as well as interesting visuals.

[b]Audio[/b]

Before i played the game, i already liked blasphemous' music. The game did not diminish that in the slightest. In terms of sound, everything makes sense, and does a good job to enhance the game's atmosphere.

[b]Bugs[/b]

Unfortunately, the game did have two bugs for me. Opening steam's overlay made the game crash, and twice, i got stuck in a death loop, forcing me to restart the game.

[b]Verdict[/b]

I would rate Blasphemous as worse than Hollow Knight, because its gameplay is worse and Hollow Knight did not have bugs. However, Blasphemous trumps Salt & Sanctuary: The gameplay, while not as varied, had a better feeling to it, and both storywise and aesthetically, it outshines its competitor. Recent reviews give it a 93%, which it well deserves.

The creators recently released a free DLC for the game, with 5 new bosses. Definitely a plus, as it is an indication that the game is not dead, and new content is being added, further increasing the value of their product.

Indie developers once again putting the entire AAA industry to shame. Atmosphere, music, locations and bosses are on point. The pixel art is beautiful, the NPCs are really good and finding the collectibles is actually rewarding. The progression is good, you gradually feel like you're becoming stronger, and the combat is fun. I have no bad things to say except F*CK the time trials and the Shipyard, thankfully they're optional.

A very fun but very flawed experience. I have the same praises as many other people: the aesthetic and the music are heart-stopping, the lore is excellent, and the world is very dense and well designed. I disagree with others who say the controls and challenges are not good, they do a really great job of emulating the classics and did not shy away from showing it. Watching The Penitent One jump just like Arthur in Ghosts n Goblins when I played the secret 8-bit minigame told me these guys know ball.

However where this game falls flat is that it feels very, for lack of a better word, "loose". The power ramp feels really weird, as in the beginning of the game is pretty difficult, and by the end you are so strong that everything feels baby-mode easy. There are tons of sidequests and characters you can meet but nothing pointing you towards them so its very hard to see everything without looking up a guide. The teleport system doesn't make any sense, and getting the upgrade that lets you teleport between save points is pretty much mandatory or you will be absolutely miserable. The animations are very lengthy and lock you into them for far too long, and mixed with the very obviously wrong hitboxes with some enemies/attacks, this leads to a lot of deaths that just don't feel fair. Very important traveling upgrades are locked behind lengthy quest chains instead of bosses or locked doors like other Metroidvanias. Lastly, I think the DLC bosses are way too overtuned, which is a shame because the main game bosses were quite good and fair. Isadora was as hard as everyone else says but the second phase of Crisanta is REALLY something else. Her first phase is the best fight in the game, so it hits you like whiplash. Even with every upgrade you can get, it just feels like everything is stacked against you, from parries pushing you too far to giving you no time to heal ever, and it feels even worse once you play the final boss afterwards and it's extremely easy in comparison. 

This game feels like a squeaky shopping cart or a car with two bad wheels: it's functional, but very annoying and your attention is constantly drawn towards it. There are so many unsanded corners and untightened screws and they are constantly making everything uncomfortable. The multitude of things wrong with this game aren't enough to make it not fun, but they were enough to take the fun out of it a few times. I stuck with it to the end and was glad I did, but this game really pushes you to both try your best and look past its glaring flaws for the moments of glory it gives you. I'm not sure if there's something to be said about suffering for glory here, but I don't think that was the game's intention. I say it's a solid 7.5/10, but be wary that it will test your patience just as much as it will test your skill.

Blasphemous is a marriage of Castlevania and Dark Souls, and often times it reaches the same highs as those two IP.  But, it also hits the same lows, sometimes even more so than the inspiration it borrows from.

I haven't been this frustrated playing a Metroidvania in a long time, on one hand you get visceral combat, arguably the most gorgeous pixel art ever put into a game, and a hauntingly macabre world on the brink of total desolation with the Miracle to blame.  The music is stellar, the character models and sprite work make Hotline Miami seem amateurish, and the gorey and brutal combat feels punchy and impactful.

But my God, this game doesn't want you to have fun with it. At times, I felt like the developer actively hated me.

1) Fast Travel is locked behind a 20,000 Tears tithe at the church. Prior to saving up this obscene amount, you have to rely on a paltry handful of portals dotted around the map.  This game came out post Dark Souls THREE, by then FROM figured out nobody wants to do Lost Izalith-tier runbacks when the game arbitrarily kills them with Bed of Chaos' trash hitboxes.  Blasphemous has no excuse for how long, excruciating and tiresome many of the runbacks are, which even when you can afford the upgrade like I did around the halfway mark, it doesn't take away the sting of having to run all that way back to collect your Guilt because you got stunlocked by gas and fell into a pit of spikes that instakilled you.

2) Enemy design is the best and worst of this game.  You get some really simple but effective gimmicks like flying enemies, stationary hazards, a Bell-wearing enemy that behaves like a raging bull.  All good.  What isn't good is the f*cking retarded shit like a corridor full of projectile spamming enemies with ghosts that fade in and out along the way that chip damage you on contact with no way for you to jump out of the way because their sprites are so tall.  The amount of deaths I had to being stunlocked, knocked down and then continuously tick-damaged as the Penitent one fails to get up made me want to strangle myself like David Carradine, minus the orgasm.

3) Crucial upgrades are many times too far out of the way of the beaten path, and worse yet, you only have 3 of these crucial upgrade slots at one time. There's no need for this. All the abilities are absolutely necessary especially in end and post-game. We should have them autoequipped as passives the moment we find them.

4) No auto-marking of collectibles you pass by.  This is QoL you got in ORI in 2014, Blasphemous has no excuse. 

5) Many questlines are vague and obtuse just because Dark Souls is vague and obtuse. You don't need to copy EVERYTHING Fromsoft does, especially when their quest design is one of the worst aspects of their games.  I got all the items I needed for the true ending by playing normally, but turns out I killed a certain boss too early, so I'm locked out of getting a key that allows me to use those key items to get a Mea Culpa upgrade and access to said ending.

6) I had to play this with a controller about 1/3 of the way through. The game, despite being in full screen, does not lock your cursor to the window and if you play KB/M you are GOING to end up clicking off the screen, especially mid-jump and end up dying. This is terrible for any PC game and shouldn't be the norm any year past 2012 when PC ports started to get refined.  If I have to use a controller for a non hack-n-slash like DMC/NG, you failed.

Is Blasphemous worth your time? Absolutely. It has a breadth of unlocks, cool bosses (except the Snake, that boss is awful), great music, brutal combat that feels like DOOM married to a Priest on a crusade against wretched Abomination, and a real feeling of progression as you play.
Would I replay it again? Maybe sometime in the future. 

Just be prepared to be very, very frustrated. The game itself is easy. I cleared most bosses on my first attempts, but traversal with the gank squads of stunlocks and chip damage are so bad I'd rather play Hollow Knight when it gets bad, and I think that game is the most Epstein-coded trash out there. Ninja Gaiden 2 on Warrior dookies all over this game's difficulty, and not one time in that game did I feel like I was devoid of any control over my victories and defeats.

But there is a major issue: [b]the game doesn't respect your time.[/b]

[spoiler]Almost all metroidvanias have multiple endings and reward exploration with additional lore, bosses and areas.
Blasphemous has multiple endings as well, and a good chunk of side content that needs to be completed to achieve the "true" ending.
This is not just achievement hunting. With metroidvanias, going for the true ending lets you explore and experience the game to its fullest and can be really rewarding.

To get the true ending, you are expected to do things in a specific order and if you don't, you get locked out of certain content. There are no real pointers about the expected order of events and it's almost impossible to get it right on your first playthrough without a guide.

There are also other "time sensitive" quests that lock you out if you don't finish them before killing certain bosses.

[b]*** THIS IS ALL PERFECTLY FINE ***[/b]

The problem is, if you don't do everything in the expected order, you end up with a bunch of non-functioning late game items and NPCs.
Since the game doesn't tell you anything about getting locked out of these questlines, you end up backtracking through the map again and again, thinking you must've missed something, only to finally give up, check online and find out that you've been wasting your time.

Everything in the game indicates that there is more to do. You still have quest items, NPC dialogues indicate there are unfinished quests, but unbeknownst to you, you are completely locked out.

It would've been fine if the items were somehow taken away from you once you messed up the order, the optional boss encounters were walled of or at least the NPCs hinted that their quests could no longer be completed. But since none of this happens, you end up losing hours looking for solutions that are not there.

There are also certain items that were added with the DLCs which can't be collected on your first playthrough even though they have placeholders in your inventory. There is also a DLC area that can't be accessed.
This once again leads to searching the map for things that are not there.

As a final quibble, some secrets are almost impossible to find through deduction alone. You either need to get lucky, hit every wall on sight or check online. 
But this is a general problem with most metroidvanias.

In the end, this game seems to be designed for multiple playthroughs.
That's fine, but there should have been ingame indicators about this design choice for players who are trying to avoid online spoilers. [/spoiler]

The pixel art, animation and world building are absolutely stellar and if that was all the game was it'd have done amazing well. But as far as actual [i]gameplay[/i] is concerned there's better. Hollow Knight being the most recent one.

Blasphemous' biggest problem is that it's a combat-focused game trying to be a platformer and just fundamentally fails. Platforming is a staple part of any good Metroidvania, sure, but that's the point: Blasphemous isn't a good Metroidvania.

Platforming is a good 90% of what the game has you do but the platforming is just straight terrible. Jumps require almost pixel-perfect positioning or you'll miss by quarter of an inch and plummet to instant death. Of which 90% of the platforming consists of. Spikes, spikes, and more spikes!

None of this is helped by the fact the controls are clunky. Controls are always hard to explain but when it comes to Blasphemous the float is too "floaty" (in that you have no real control over it), you often do not grab ladders when needed to while you [i]constantly[/i] grab ledges when trying to get below them. Worse is that the button to attach to a wall is the same as your attack key, so there's a good chance you'll either stick to the wall when you want to attack a flying enemy (or do a downward attack) or you'll attack when you want to stick instead.

Aside from this the game simply has no respect for your time. Checkpoints are few and far between and the "fast-travel" system is practically non-existent and in some cases it's one-way, so if you didn't know it was a shortcut and need to go back well good luck, you've gotta run through the whole bloody game again.

The other major waste of time comes from the inability to pan the camera down far enough, and in some areas you just can't pan down at all. The game requires too many leaps of faith; areas where you have to wait and fall to a platform below you that you cannot pan down and see so you don't actually know if it's there or not. Fail and you return all the way to the last checkpoint, which is often behind numerous traps and enemies.

The combat, on the other hand, is great. The parry is extremely potent, perhaps even too forgiving, while the actual combos and dodge feel great. My only complaint is doing the dodge-attack combo would feel better if you could activate it mid-dodge rather than having to activate it immediately after dodging, but other than that it's great.

...Except when you have to fight [i]and[/i] platform at the same time. Then it's pretty much impossible. The game does this a lot, and it's not helped by the fact that fighting more than one enemy is extremely difficult as many will fly and teleport around the room while you're confined to the very flat, very 2D plane you move on.

All this would be more acceptable if you were amply rewarded but you're not. Relics and spells are things you have to actually look quite hard for. Unlike most Metroidvania's you're never really blocked by a major obstacle that needs specific gear to progress. You will very likely miss a large amount of useful items on your first run purely because you don't know where they are. Some of these are useful, such as ridding you of the toxic cloud poison crap. Progress to new areas is opened up purely by boss fights and gear is pretty much non-existent for much of the run.

Blasphemous is overall not worth the $30. There's just way too many platforming/Metroidvania-style indie titles at a similar price point that all have far less issues. If the platforming wasn't so unforgiving (90% of your deaths will be from the environment) and the checkpoints not so few the game wouldn't feel nearly as bad, but as it stands Blasphemous is a terrible game that makes you feel like you've done nothing but waste hours getting nowhere.

The game has a phenomenal atmosphere, amazing location soundtracks, and a great Dark Souls-style lore delivery. 

However, it can feel incredibly tedious at times. The backtracking is overwhelming, fast-travel portals are highly non-obvious and cost a ridiculous 20k Tears, and the instant-death spikes are infuriating. Dying to spikes means you have to run through hordes of enemies all over again, which led me to uninstall and quit the game several times. 

Ultimately, I pushed through and finished it. Despite all the frustration, I would still recommend it to fans of the genre.

After 16 hours, I beat Blasphemous and got the true ending. Here are my thoughts.

Blasphemous is a hardcore platforming metroidvania game with a dark theme and setting. The artwork in this game draws heavily from Spanish renaissance paintings and religious works, and is truly a unique and beautiful game despite the pixel medium. The game has a surprising amount of cutscenes given the detail and effort that must have gone into them, I think I counted around 7-10 during my playthrough. The story is vague and alien with most of the lore being hidden in item incredibly detailed item descriptions giving insight into a particular topic, which works to the game's favor by adding in a mysterious and ominous feeling (think Hollow Knight or Dark Souls). 

The enemy design and basic combat are fun and engaging. Many enemies feel unique, and their frame by frame drawn animations make every encounter feel good. With a controller (which I highly recommend to anyone playing) each hit causes the controller to vibrate just a little, making it really seem like there's some weight to your swings.

Despite the unique and deep world to explore and tame, as well as the absolutely astounding artwork (some scenes in the game must have taken weeks to draw, it's honestly crazy) the game's flaws come from the actual gameplay.

As a souls veteran, I'm no stranger to difficult experiences, but a few hours into the game, the difficulty had jumped from easy to incredibly difficult. I had been wandering a swamp filled with mindless monk enemies that took a mere few swings to fell, and had ended up in snowy peaks where leech-men and bell ghost things were making short work of me in a matter of seconds. Nevertheless I persisted and defeated one of the three bosses the game sets you up to face. Next I ventured down into a strange chasm filled with chains and bells, and defeated my next boss. As I went on though, I realised through the help of the steam global achievements that I had defeated the hardest two of the three bosses, and upon meeting the final foe of the trio, I first tried him. I think this helps to show that the level design can be a little confusing, I mistook the obvious hard difficulty as intended, and as a result was much more powerful than you're meant to be when fighting the first real boss of the game, so I think some better indicators of where you're meant to go could be needed, then again this is my experience alone.

My second gripe with the game is the combat, and let me tell you; skills are basically useless. I found myself almost never utilising any skills outside of my basic attacks, basic dodges and parries the entire game. The charge attack feels useless, you essentially always get hit when charging it up, and the payoff is lackluster, as you do the same amount of damage with the combo skill: a useful skill, it's upgrades are a bit useless though as again, they seem to do the same amount of damage. The long range skill is also useful, you need it for collectibles and you can dispatch enemies easily, but outside of the basic combo skill and ranged attack, the plunge, dodge-thrust as well as their various upgrades feel more troublesome than they're worth.

And to emphasise: [b] I never managed to pull off a plunging attack once in my 16 hours of gameplay. [/b]

I don't know if I'm stupid or what, but the instructions for the attack - down + attack - are useless, I sat for a good five minutes every now and then trying to pull one off, I couldn't even managing it when my character was falling down a huge well!

The map system also is a big drawback for me. A lot of the areas and items you'll encounter initially will require a relic - an item that "shapes reality" by creating platforms or allowing you to move in a hazard - in order to reach them, and some relics are very confusing to obtain (the three tongues relic required a lot of thinking for me). While this wouldn't be a problem initially, once you realise that all the items and moonlight babies you missed are invisible on the map, you'll have to search entire areas should your memory fail you in order to get those juicy collectibles, an issue that could be fixed either by enabling the player to mark the map manually with an X, or by adding in a pin system akin to Hollow Knight. But really though. Imagine playing Hollow Knight with no pins. It's like that.

The last gripe I had with the game is that the bosses are sometimes disappointing. I found myself in late game areas fighting a boss and killing it on my first or second attempt, and with the upgrade system requiring you to search areas for upgrades rather than spending money to level up, I wasn't even overleveled for the encounter. That being said, many of the bosses still have a lot of effort put into them both in terms of animations and mechanics (seriously the archbishop was my favorite boss by far), but for me a lot of the challenge was missing, especially on the final boss which was pretty disappointing difficulty wise for the climactic final fight of the game.

All in all, Blasphemous was a unique and pretty fun experience, and despite the flaws present in the game, I'd still recommend it to fans of the genre. I'd give it a 8/10. The art, theme and soul of the game really really carry it for me.

EDIT (Minor Spoilers): Another thing I've realised, as far as the endings go, it's a pretty big oof. The "true ending" of the game is incredibly hidden, and I don't necessarily mind that, I do mind however how the "normal" ending is absolutely [spoiler] brutal and crushing. It feels like a kick in the face compared to the true ending! [/spoiler]

You know, in a weird way this game really made me appreciate my faith in Christ even more lol. The predominant theme in this game is suffering, all to atone for your sins and appeal to the whims of some capricious, eldritch force called the Miracle. No matter what you do, though, your absolution is never guaranteed, and whether you do receive absolution or punishment, the end result is the same: more suffering, more pleading, never certain whether "enough" is enough, only watching as you deteriorate along with the rest of the world subject to the same cruel force. 

An enshrinement of transactional suffering and worship of a force that ultimately doesn't really seem to care about you.

Not so with Christ, who suffered for us so that we might not have to suffer, and who through His death and resurrection, guaranteed the atonement of our sins so that we might be reconciled to Him, a God who truly does care about us, hears us, and desires the best for us. 

Theological musings aside, though, this is a great game. I've never played too many Metroidvanias—my main one is Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, which sets a pretty high bar that Blasphemous is able to meet. The environmental imagery is grotesque in many ways but still evocative and beautiful due to its inspiration from Catholic Christian imagery and architecture. Each area successfully manages to create a feeling of foreboding, sorrow, reverence, and even adventure, due in no small part to the music. The music is definitely one of my favorite things about the game, and it really made me appreciate traditional Spanish music... something that's a bit personally relevant to me after growing up being exposed to Hispanic music styles like salsa, reggaeton, and norteña that I largely found obnoxious and grating. 

Obviously, music is largely a matter of taste, but it really was nice finally being exposed to a Hispanic musical style I actually really liked.

Being a Spanish speaker, I set the language (audio and text) to Spanish and was impressed by how good the voice acting was and how many new, if potentially archaic, words I learned lol. Even if you don't speak Spanish, you should definitely set it to Spanish still and just have the text in English, because the voice acting really does a lot for immersion and creating that feeling of being in an old, noble, and "foreign" place.

Finally, the gameplay. Movement is simplistic in design since it is a 2D game, but it doesn't feel clunky or outdated and instead feels smooth and responsive. Combat, mainly when it comes to the bosses, is challenging but fair, and it was fun figuring out their movesets to finally get a clean (clean enough at least lol) win in.

My main advice when it comes to exploration would be to make good use of the map marking system, because there will be PLENTY of areas and items that are inaccessible until much later in the game once you've unlocked  the necessary powerup to reach them. It's a fairly large map, too, so don't count on yourself to remember exactly what you missed and where.

The Grievous Miracle has caused the faithful and the sinner to manifest their deeds physically, onto their bodies, turning the pious into angelic saints and the sinful into hideous fiends. Now, go forth, Penitent One, and complete your penance if you are worthy.

From the title screen to the animations, enemies, bosses and voice acting.. Holy! This game is in its own league and well deserves its praise. It's enveloping, challenging and disturbing in a good way with an insane amount of lore. The environments to explore are some of the best I've seen in a Metroidvania. Gameplay wise, it's not boring and just feels really good to play with a plethora of things to find and customize for your build.

If you're on the fence about this game, I strongly recommend it, especially if you're into occult, religion, or esoteric and philosophy; there's nothing quite like it that captures these themes and aesthetics.

The colors, the art, the setting and the lore are spectacular. The voice acting is also very good. Deeply based on religious iconography and themes while being cautious of crossing the line, [i]Blasphemous[/i]’ unsettling mood and painstaking detail to everything visual will stay with you for a long time.

This is a pixel-art game that fully exploits modern hardware and design, thankfully moving away from the lazy trend of blurry 2D games in imitation of those primitive 8-bit-era graphics that today look dated and dysfunctional.

The player character, known only as the Penitent One, is a taciturn creature with little personality but what he lacks in dialogue is compensated by the rich explanations provided by NPCs and in-game elements.

Movement is fluid and responsive, and combos are satisfying and finishers gruesomely rewarding, but there is little variation. The combat feeling is solid. The difficulty is moderately hard, but fair. It will gradually become easier once you understand the mechanics of enemies. This is not a game where button mashing will get you very far. I strongly recommend the use of a gamepad. I played with the XBox One wireless controller, which is fully supported. I did not encounter a single bug or glitch.

A small but very important detail that I liked a lot is that the game teaches you its mechanics in a smooth way, slowly as you progress through the first stages. No enemy or monster is introduced without proper warning, and the very first of its kind that you see allows for observation and experimentation without too much nearby danger. This is the way all games should be made—no need for dedicated, irrelevant, boring and lengthy tutorials.

There's lots to see and discover, and this is a game to enjoy and take your time to observe. The art is fantastic, and it is seamlessly integrated with the game's mechanics. You might end up wanting to know more about the bizarre enemies, strange locations and intriguing NPCs. Yet, if you want to savor [i]Blasphemous[/i], there will be a moderate amount of reading involved. Some fragments of lore are a bit confusing, but worth your attention if you are looking to complete all quests or hunt for achievements.

Backtracking is abundant, but I found the process not as tiresome or tedious as some other people refer. Mainly because it is a pleasure to see again those gorgeous backgrounds and art, and change the setting every now and then. One thing that must be applauded is that the game manages to keep the sense of discovery fresh. Each new area is as impressive as the last.

[i]Blasphemous[/i] is a game that rewards experimentation and curiosity, but it also punishes them in the same measure—an intriguing component definitely in line with the theme of penance and suffering. 

I don't know about "metroidvanias" of yore since I never played them, but another comparison that usually arises is to Dark Souls. Yes, some elements are similar, like the endless cycle of death and rebirth, learning along the way, but [i]Blasphemous[/i] is not as hard or frustrating. Upon dying all items are kept, but the performance of the Penitent One will decrease until you recover your soul at the place of your demise. This mechanic keeps things interesting while adding another layer of simple strategy.

The bosses are impressive and varied, likely to pose a challenge to the unprepared. In the end, like the game itself, they can be defeated by learning the patterns and skillfully dodging their attacks. The bosses' visual design is the crown jewel of the already outstanding work of the developers in this area.

The map is huge, and the different areas are clearly distinct from one another in theme and ambience. Sometimes you need to move from one place to the other and the journey will be a bit too long. There are fast-travel portals and some other convenience-aimed devices—so the developers are aware of this—but maybe not enough. Still, [i]Blasphemous[/i]’ map is designed in a way that it allows for surprising shortcuts and interesting transitions. Also, be aware that there are lots of secret rooms.

Sound edition is good. The music is nice, and helps set the proper dark ambience. Its main problem is, of course, that it becomes repetitive very quickly. This is a usual affliction of the genre, since they rely on infinite looping, and only extremely long tracks would solve the issue.

There’s much more to [i]Blasphemous[/i] that can be seen at first glance: a dark mythology based on distressing—but detailed and unusual traditions. There is a lot of philosophy concerned between lines in this fantastical tale. What strikes me is the perspective of the reality that inspires the myth and fuels the story in the game. Maybe, like me, you will end up reflecting about the world’s values and the validity of beliefs. This is a triumph for a game like this; a breath of fresh air among many other half-baked, brain-dead platformers.

A good game that dares to be bold and succeeds. It will suck your afternoon if you allow it to, in a fun way. Be prepared to die and repeat a lot of sections.

I can't wait to see what these guys at The Game Kitchen are up to next.

Piously recommended.
