Executing enemies giving temporary I-Frames and being visually appealing but after a while you might prefer to be faster and end them normally. A variety of items for your swords, open world interactivity, and buffs make exploration worth doing.

The platforming is solid, ladders can be a bit iffy at times and spike traps can have deceptively longer reach than what's shown visually. While platforming is a big part of the game and isn't too hard in my opinion that all changes for the Miriam Challenges. A series of 5 platforming challenges that feel out of place in this game, while I did say platforming is huge, it never felt meant to be played as a "platformer" to me. These challenges were overly annoying, needing you to have certain prayers, cheese and just really know the mechanics of the game. Aside from being timed, it feels like a trial and error that will likely take you more time doing than just playing and beating the game. Combined with a lackluster reward for your struggles, I probably wouldn't do them ever again on future playthroughs.

Bosses were challenging but never felt unbeatable, but some bosses and content are only on NG+. Which adds a bit more to the game in terms of content, along with the only way to get the "True" ending. You lose most things when going into NG+ but you keep your sword upgrades, Prayers, and some items, everything else has to be reacquired. In NG+ you can choose from a few penalties to go through the game to add an extra challenge, if you beat the game with it on you get a playable character skin, penalties can be removed if you want them off. You can unlock character skins by doing various things or challenges.

Overall I really liked Blasphemous and would recommend it to anyone who likes a bit of a challenge and metroid-vania style games. It kept me engaged and pushing onward for the sake of the sake and adventure. But it can be vague in certain key areas and you'll be reaching in the dark to figure things out unless by chance or looking it up. So the majority of players won't be able to experience many things I feel, along with the Miriam challenges being tedious. Having quests or endings being very specific mean future runs become more stream-lined if you want a certain outcome, needing to do or don't.

While I personally enjoyed it, I can see why others may not or have struggles playing it and for that I give it a 8/10

Blasphemous is a game I have been anxiously waiting for its completion since the day they launched their Kickstarter page. Now the game is finally out, and I say it goes beyond my expectation. I cherish every moment in my playthrough. 

As the penitent one, player must journey through Cvstodia to purge the land of its guilt, but your bloody and violent pilgrimage will not be easy. Various foes will try to stop you at all cost. Blasphemous delivers the sorrow tone of dread through breathtaking pixel art that undoubtedly could even rival some 3D games. Every scene and settings contain a silent story told through your progression, being a snowy mountain with statues of weeping nuns or a grand cathedral with bells and incenses swaying in a solemn hallway. The best company for such mysterious world is a wonderful background music. If you pay attention to the music, you can hear a reoccuring tone throughout each soundtrack. This idea to my opinion reinforces the interconnected world. You might be in a snowy peak or deep down the catacomb, but in the end you are always be in Cvstodia. The combat is simple—a guilt-cleansing sword by your hand to swipe through sinners and sinner-likes. Various items,  magics and combat skills for you to further customizing The Penitent One on the journey.  

The game is good, but that does not mean it contains zero flaw. At the store page, the game promotes itself as a “punishing action-platformer”. You might assume the statement refers to the unrelenting enemies across the holy land. The truth is, that your nemesis is neither bosses nor minions, but the spike traps. I satirically acclaim this game as “pixel-perfect” as it can be. What I really mean the platforming requires you to be pixel perfect. Just imagine you have to hover right foot over the spike in order to perform a successful jump. Most of my death come from spikes just because I am a tiny pixel away from plunging into my doom. Another is a minor complaint. The parry frame is too generous. You can parry any attacks as long as the sword is still over your head. This fact drastically reduces the difficulty of the game and even renders some boss fights trivial. 

All in all, the experience is pleasant. The developer of The Last Door manages to deliver another great pixel game with depth and gameplay. I definitely recommend it.

I originally tried to play Blasphemous in late 2023, but gave up about 2 1/2 hours because of some frustrating game design issues and because I just wasn't having much fun. Fast forward to mid 2025, and I finally tried the game again. I ended up enjoying it more this time around, giving the game more of a chance and spending some time on it. However, after having completed it now and finishing most of the map, I still can't really recommend Blasphemous, mostly because it still isn't really all that fun and has some game design flaws.

Here is what I will say about Blasphemous: it drips with style. The pixel art is gorgeous, the soundtrack is haunting and the game isn't afraid to toss around gore like confetti at a kid's birthday party. It has a theme and sticks to it very well, and it makes you want to learn more about the world. Sadly, games are meant to be played (for the most part), not just looked at, but Blasphemous would win just based on style if that was the case.

It's kind of a mixture of a souls-like and a metroidvania. You have a limited amount of flasks you regenerate at certain shrines, and if you die, you respawn at those shrines and have to walk back to your corpse to regenerate some of your stats. It's fairly standard, and mostly unproblematic, because Blasphemous isn't all that hard in terms of gameplay. Most bosses can be spam-attacked to death and outhealed easily, aside from very few that spike the difficulty randomly (a true souls-like indeed) and most of your deaths will come from environmental hazards or enemies that knock you off of tiny platforms and into spikes. Overall, it doesn't really reinvent the wheel and the souls-like aspect is fine, if a bit unnecessary and just serves to lengthen an already short-ish game.

What caused me not to recommend it is the metroidvania aspect of it. Even being done with the game, and with most of the map uncovered (over 90 %) I still have not found quite a few objects and rooms because the things I need to reach them (presumably), I still have not found. I looked it up and it turns out you need to do a series of fetch quests that you can easily miss, for NPCs you will not remember the moment you leave the room because you have other things to do and that are not marked on the map, with items you will not find until hours later. It's incredibly unsatisfying and so the main draw of a metroidvania was not happening in my playthrough, because the items needed for that are obscurely tucked away behind layers of brick, and only god knows where the sledgehammer is. It's bafflingly annoying and I would go as far as to say it's barely even a metroidvania at all, despite those small rooms and areas being shoved into your face so often during your playthrough, only for you to likely never reach them unless you're lucky or follow a guide. It's the antithesis of what makes a metroidvania fun.

Many items are barely explained and only used for quests, the map is absolutely terrible for a metroidvania (NPCs not marked, blood fountains that are already used for new flasks aren't marked as complete and still look like they can be used on the map, etc. etc. etc.) It's like the convoluted lore for a souls game, but transferred into the gameplay - not that the lore and story for Blasphemous aren't convoluted, because they are about as nonsensical as you would expect, though they provide a cool background for your gameplay.

I guess that would be the last aspect to take a look at - how does the game play? You attack with a sword, and you only get very few attacks over the course of the game. There are a few powers that use your fervor gauge, and your combo may expand at some point, and you get a sliding attack, but the gameplay remains fairly one-dimensional, causing boredom long before you reach the end of the game. Many attacks beyond just a simple sword swing lock you into long animations, which is a problem - you never need to use them outside of bosses, but they kill you when used with most bosses. I wish there were more weapons, or more attack styles.

I played quite a few souls-likes and metroidvanias that I really enjoyed over the years, and even recently. Blasphemous just doesn't do either well, in my opinion. The map is too big, the game is too repetitive, the metroidvania aspect is badly implemented with a hard-to-read and uninformative map, and it doesn't reach the satisfaction a souls-like should. When it was over, I was just glad more than anything, but not really satisfied. On a huge sale, it might be worth a look if just for the style and some of the cool areas and bosses, but if you want to have fun playing, there are far better games of its genres available.

I played the demo of Blasphemous a couple weeks back and immediately fell in love with the absolutely gorgeous artwork and amazing atmosphere of the game.  Tonight I finished the true ending and all the challenges in Strife & Ruin. There are some games you know will stick with you, and this is one of them for me.

As you could probably tell from the trailer or countless other reviews, Blasphemous is a platformer metroidvania set in a dark, fantastical world of Christian themes. Picture walking through the fevered nightmares of Torquemada, complete with twisted medieval Spanish landscapes, towering cathedrals, and forgotten crypts.  There's no denying that the art, music, and overall atmosphere of the game are superbly realized - serious kudos to everyone involved. Even when you're retracing your steps across the same areas after (another) death, experiencing the game world around you makes it totally worth it. I was always really excited to encounter a new boss, just to see the larger-than-life art in store for me.

Blasphemous is also difficult, but with a few exception, I didn't think it was as hard as comparable platformers like Hollow Knight. After a little while of game play and buffing a bit, I rarely died from damage. The biggest source of death (and this is a common theme in the reviews) are the lovely spike pits, but for me, there were really only a couple areas where I consistently died from them (looking at you, Sleeping Canvases). And often times this was due to my impatience or stupid mistakes.  Some of the bosses were also tricky, but I can't say any of them took more than 5-6 tries for me.  Though my play style tends to be to collect as many powerups as possible before heading into a boss battle, so that may have affected the outcome.

And if you want a platforming challenge, the Strife and Ruin expansion will not disappoint (though if you're like me, prepare for some serious frustration). With only 5 challenges, it's not huge amount of additional content, but the last 3 of those challenge took a good amount of practice to conquer, the last was probably 25-30 retries.  

I do feel like Blasphemous has some game play issues.  Jumping ladder grabs and ledge grabs seem off in opposite ways.  You must hit up exactly at the right time when jumping past a ladder, or you will miss it. The Strife and Ruin expansions will make this abundantly apparent if you didn't realize it already. I wish so, so much that you could just hold down up and it would auto-grab as you passed it.  And ledge grabs happen all the time, whether you want them to or not. If there's a ledge on the screen, there is a 95% chance you will be hanging from it very soon. Also, small thing, but I wish the sword bounce didn't use the same directions as the downward thrust, this burned me on multiple occasions as well (again, especially in Strife and Ruin).  Lastly, there are some cheap moments when multiple attacks are positioned in some way that don't allow recovery.  But honestly, I feel like this is par for the course in many platformers.

That being said though, I feel the positives of this game vastly outweigh those frustrating moments.  There is lots to explore, secrets to find, powers to unlock, enemies to battle (and many ways to kill them) - basically all the stuff metroidvania fans like myself love. And it's a beautiful and haunting experience the entire way.  If you like the genre and are up for a little punishment, definitely pick this one up!

The game is just very pleasant for eyes, ears and fingers. I would personally rate it 8.5/10.
It starts out slowly and lets you learn its mechanics but you will be dashing and slashing your way through before you know it. The combat is fluent and, in some occasions, pretty fast paced.
The game isn't really hard and you will kill most of the bosses on your first or second try. There are plenty of spells to adjust to your play style, plenty of power-ups and upgrades to make your exploration worthwhile, plenty of collectibles to keep you busy and give you extra few hours of gameplay and a couple of puzzles with big rewards behind them that will make you very satisfied if you solve them on your own. So Blasphemous is definitely not a game where you just play it speed-running throughout the entire levels (it is the way it’s supposed to be played) so a lot of patience would be required if you want to enjoy the game fully.
I cannot say much about the story without spoiling it. I can only say it's brutal, dramatic and original, and the way it is told just makes it even more interesting.
The visuals in my honest opinion are great and I believe most Metroid-Vania fans will agree, but not everyone is fan of such grotesque pixel art. every place feels special and unique whether because of the ambiance, the music or even the enemies, and the level design's variety helps taking advantage of the character's movements and controls perfectly.
There are, of course some flaws which I would like to point out: lack of enemy variety; lack of difficulty and replay value.
However, those flaws are nothing compared to the great content that Blasphemous offers you.
Blasphemous tries, and succeeds in being as original as it can, and is one truly beautiful experience.
